\chapter{Building a Paragraph --- Plan, Add, Join, Refer Back}
\label{ch:parrafo}
\hlchaptermodality{273}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can build a paragraph in Spanish whose sentences signal how they relate to one another, and say what is lost when the signals are removed.}

Complete ES-C273-practice: build a four-sentence paragraph with each join, then say it again with the joins removed and describe what changed.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[en primer lugar]{en primer lugar — telling the reader the shape before you fill it}

\label{lesson:ES-C273-en-primer-lugar}



\begin{quote}
You can build a sentence that means more than it says. This chapter is about building something longer than a sentence.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item mira — the marker that re-tunes what follows.
  \item por ejemplo — the evidence move.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{en pri-MER lu-GAR}. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{en primer lugar} — \textquotedblleft{}in the first place, firstly.\textquotedblright{}

\emph{Primer} is Latin \textbf{primarius}, \textquotedblleft{}of the first rank\textquotedblright{} — English \textbf{primary}, \textbf{prime}. \emph{Lugar} is \textbf{locus}, \textquotedblleft{}place\textquotedblright{} — English \textbf{local}, \textbf{locate}. Literally: \emph{in the first place}, and English kept the phrase intact.

Its partners are \emph{en segundo lugar} and \emph{por último}, \textquotedblleft{}lastly.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
This is not a connective. It does not join two ideas — it tells the listener \textbf{how many are coming}.

That is a different job, and it is what makes extended text followable. A reader who hears \emph{en primer lugar} knows to expect a second point and holds a slot open for it. Take the phrase away and the same three points arrive as an undifferentiated list.

Signposting is most of what separates a paragraph from a pile of sentences.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{en primer lugar} and make a point
  \item \emph{en segundo lugar} and make another
  \item \emph{por último} and close
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What Latin words are inside \emph{primer} and \emph{lugar}? (\emph{Primarius} and \emph{locus}.) What does the phrase tell a listener that a connective does not? (How many points are coming.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[además]{además — adding a point, not adding an item}

\label{lesson:ES-C273-ademas}



\begin{quote}
You have \emph{también}, "also." This is not the same word, and the difference is the same one \emph{pero} and \emph{sin embargo} had.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item en primer lugar — the signpost before this.
  \item también — the \textquotedblleft{}also\textquotedblright{} you already own.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{a-de-MÁS}, and the accent tells you so. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{además} — \textquotedblleft{}furthermore, moreover, besides.\textquotedblright{}

Take it apart: \emph{a} + \emph{de} + \emph{más} — \textquotedblleft{}to, of, more.\textquotedblright{} It is built out of three words you already have, and \emph{más} is the comparison word from the experience chapter.

So it means, quite literally, \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}in addition to more.\textquotedblright{}} Spanish built its heaviest additive connector out of its lightest pieces.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\emph{También} adds an \textbf{item}: \emph{hablo español; también hablo francés.} \emph{Además} adds a \textbf{point}: \emph{es difícil. Además, es caro.}

The first says \emph{one more of the same kind}. The second says \emph{and here is a further reason}, and it is what an argument uses when the reasons are not interchangeable.

That is the same distinction you met with \emph{pero} and \emph{sin embargo}: the light word joins inside a breath, the heavy one opens a new sentence and carries argumentative weight.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item two like items with \emph{también}
  \item two separate reasons with \emph{además}
  \item which of the two an argument needs, and why
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What three words is \emph{además} built from? (\emph{A}, \emph{de}, \emph{más}.) What does \emph{también} add, and what does \emph{además} add? (An item; a point.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[por lo tanto]{por lo tanto — the word that makes a text hold together}

\label{lesson:ES-C273-por-lo-tanto}



\begin{quote}
Signpost, addition — and now the join that turns a list of points into an argument.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item además — adding a further point.
  \item así que — the everyday \textquotedblleft{}so\textquotedblright{} you already have.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{por lo TAN-to}. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{por lo tanto} — \textquotedblleft{}therefore, consequently.\textquotedblright{}

\emph{Tanto} is Latin \textbf{tantus}, \textquotedblleft{}so much, so great.\textquotedblright{} The phrase is \emph{for so much} — \emph{given all that}, therefore.

You already have \emph{así que}, which does the same job in conversation. \emph{Por lo tanto} is its written, weight-bearing form: the one that appears in an argument where the conclusion has to look earned.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Here is the thing this chapter is really about. The English word for what these connectives create is \textbf{cohesion} — the property that makes a text feel like one thing rather than several.

Cohesion is not achieved by the sentences being about the same topic. It is achieved by each sentence carrying an explicit signal of \textbf{how it relates to the last one}: another point (\emph{además}), a consequence (\emph{por lo tanto}), a concession (\emph{sin embargo}), an example (\emph{por ejemplo}).

Remove those signals and a paragraph does not become wrong. It becomes work.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a claim, then \emph{por lo tanto}, then its consequence
  \item the same pair with \emph{así que}, and hear the register drop
  \item what cohesion is, in your own words
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{tanto} mean, and which Latin word is it? (So much — \emph{tantus}.) What is cohesion? (Each sentence signalling how it relates to the last.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[lo cual]{lo cual — pointing back at everything you just said}

\label{lesson:ES-C273-lo-cual}



\begin{quote}
The last piece: a way to refer to a whole idea rather than a thing.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item por lo tanto — the cohesion join.
  \item lo que — naming a thing you cannot name.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{lo KUAL}. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{lo cual} — \textquotedblleft{}which\textquotedblright{}, where the \emph{which} points at an entire preceding clause.

\emph{Cual} is Latin \textbf{qualis}, \textquotedblleft{}of what kind\textquotedblright{} — English \textbf{quality} and the \emph{-al} of \textbf{equal}. The neuter \emph{lo} in front is what widens its target: not a noun, but everything just said.

\emph{Llegó tarde, lo cual me sorprendió.} — \textquotedblleft{}He arrived late, \textbf{which} surprised me.\textquotedblright{} What surprised me is not \emph{he}, and not \emph{late}. It is the whole fact.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Pointing back at something already said is called \textbf{anaphora}, and it is the other half of cohesion. Connectives say how sentences relate; anaphora lets a sentence pick up what came before without repeating it.

Spanish is precise here in a way English is not. English \emph{which} can point at a noun or a clause and leaves you to work out which. Spanish splits the job: \emph{que} and \emph{el cual} take a noun, \emph{lo cual} takes the whole idea. The neuter \emph{lo} is the marker that says \textquotedblleft{}what follows refers to no single thing.\textquotedblright{}

With that, the chapter's four pieces are complete: plan the text, add to it, join it, and refer back within it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a sentence, then \emph{lo cual}, then your reaction to the whole of it
  \item what \emph{lo cual} points at that \emph{que} cannot
  \item the word for pointing back (\emph{anaphora})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What Latin word is \emph{cual}? (\emph{Qualis}, \textquotedblleft{}of what kind.\textquotedblright{}) What does the neuter \emph{lo} do to its target? (Widens it from a noun to a whole idea.) What is the name for pointing back? (Anaphora.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{One paragraph, four joins}

\label{lesson:ES-C273-practice}



\begin{quote}
Four pieces, and the point of them is that they only show their value at length. A single sentence never needed any of this.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Build one paragraph out loud, on any opinion you hold. Four sentences, each with its join.

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{en primer lugar}, and your first reason. The listener now knows more is coming.
  \item \emph{además}, and a second reason that is \textbf{not} the same kind as the first. If it could have taken \emph{también}, choose a different reason.
  \item \emph{por lo tanto}, and the conclusion those two reasons earn.
  \item one more sentence ending in \emph{lo cual} plus your reaction to the whole of it.
\end{itemize}

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the same four sentences again with every join REMOVED. Same content, same order.
  \item what changed. Nothing became wrong — it became work.
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of the four tells the listener how many points are coming? (\emph{En primer lugar}.) Which one points back at a whole idea? (\emph{Lo cual}.) What is the name for a text whose sentences signal how they relate? (Cohesive.)
\end{tcolorbox}
